questionText:
A student has incorrectly identified the branches of chemistry according to the descriptions given in his assignment.
Read the descriptions carefully and write the correct name of the branch of chemistry in the next column.
1. A subfield of chemistry dealing with radioactivity. It includes the study of the production and use of radioactive sources for a range of processes. (Incorrect: Physical Chemistry)
2. The study of chemical processes within and relating to living organisms. (Incorrect: Environmental Chemistry)
3. It deals with the qualitative and quantitative determination of chemical components of substances. (Incorrect: Organic Chemistry)
4. The branch of chemistry which applies physical and chemical processes for the transformation of raw materials into products on a large scale that are of benefit to humanity. (Incorrect: Nuclear Chemistry)
sloText: Define chemistry and identify its major branches (physical, organic, inorganic, analytical, biochemistry, industrial, nuclear and environmental chemistry).
checkingHints: 1 mark for each correctly identified branch of chemistry (total 4 marks):
1. Nuclear Chemistry
2. Biochemistry
3. Analytical Chemistry
4. Industrial Chemistry

rubric.description: Identifies S. No. 1 (study of radioactivity and radioactive sources) as Nuclear Chemistry.
Identifies S. No. 2 (chemical processes within living organisms) as Biochemistry.
Identifies S. No. 3 (qualitative and quantitative determination of components) as Analytical Chemistry.
Identifies S. No. 4 (large-scale transformation of raw materials into commercial products) as Industrial Chemistry.

modelAnswer:
Correct Names of the Branches of Chemistry:
1. Nuclear Chemistry (deals with radioactivity, nuclear transformations, and radioactive isotopes).
2. Biochemistry (deals with chemical structures, metabolism, and processes occurring inside living organisms).
3. Analytical Chemistry (deals with the qualitative identification and quantitative measurement of chemical components in substances).
4. Industrial Chemistry (deals with the large-scale commercial manufacturing of useful chemical products from raw materials).

questionText:
An atom of an element X has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. It loses 2 electrons from its outer most shell and acquires a +2 charge.
Draw the atomic structure of the ion of element X.
sloText: Draw the atomic structure of the first twenty elements of the periodic table and their ions using their atomic and mass numbers.
checkingHints: 1 mark for drawing the central nucleus showing 12 protons (p = 12) and 12 neutrons (n = 24 - 12 = 12).
1 mark for drawing two concentric electron shells (K shell with 2 electrons, L shell with 8 electrons; total 10 electrons).
1 mark for enclosing the ion in square brackets with a +2 charge at the top right corner: [X]^2+ or [Mg]^2+.

rubric.description: Central nucleus labeled with p = 12 and n = 12.
Two concentric shells containing 2 electrons in K-shell and 8 electrons in L-shell (valence M-shell emptied).
Square brackets around the structure with a +2 superscript ionic charge.

modelAnswer:
Atomic Structure of Ion X^(2+) (Magnesium Ion, Mg^(2+)):
1. Subatomic Particle Count:
- Atomic number (Z) = 12 => Protons (p) = 12
- Mass number (A) = 24 => Neutrons (n) = 24 - 12 = 12
- Neutral atom electrons = 12 (Configuration: K = 2, L = 8, M = 2)
- After losing 2 valence electrons from the outermost M-shell, the Mg^(2+) ion has 10 electrons (Configuration: K = 2, L = 8).

2. Structural Diagram Features:
- Central nucleus containing [ p = 12, n = 12 ].
- First shell (K-shell): 2 electrons (drawn as a pair of dots).
- Second shell (L-shell): 8 electrons (drawn as four pairs of dots).
- Entire structure enclosed in square brackets with a '+2' charge written outside at the top right: [ Mg ]^(2+).

questionText:
a. Define electronegativity. (1 Mark)
b. Describe with reasons,
i. the change in electronegativity across the period in the periodic table. (2 Marks)
ii. the trend in shielding effect when going down a group of the periodic table. (2 Marks)
sloText: Define electronegativity and explain the periodic trends in electronegativity and shielding effect across a period and down a group.
checkingHints: Part a (1 mark): Ability/tendency of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a covalent molecule.

Part b.i (2 marks): 1 mark for stating electronegativity increases across a period from left to right; 1 mark for reason (nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases while shielding remains constant).

Part b.ii (2 marks): 1 mark for stating shielding effect increases down a group; 1 mark for reason (addition of new electron shells increases the number of inner core electrons between nucleus and valence shell).

rubric.description: Part a: Defines electronegativity as the ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons in a molecule.
Part b.i: States that electronegativity increases across a period.
Part b.i: Explains reason—increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic size attract shared electrons more strongly.
Part b.ii: States that shielding effect increases going down a group.
Part b.ii: Explains reason—addition of new principal energy shells increases inner-shell electrons.

modelAnswer:
a. Definition of Electronegativity:
Electronegativity is defined as the relative ability or tendency of a bonded atom in a covalent molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself.

b.i. Change in Electronegativity Across a Period:
- Trend: Electronegativity increases when moving from left to right across a period in the periodic table.
- Reason: As we move across a period, the nuclear charge (number of protons) increases progressively while electrons are added to the same outermost shell (constant shielding effect). This increases the effective nuclear charge and shrinks the atomic radius, enabling the nucleus to attract shared bonding electrons more strongly.

b.ii. Trend in Shielding Effect Down a Group:
- Trend: The shielding (screening) effect increases when going down a group from top to bottom.
- Reason: Moving down a group, a new principal energy shell of electrons is added at each successive period. The increased number of inner-shell (core) electrons between the nucleus and the valence shell repels the outer electrons and screens them more effectively from the attractive pull of the nucleus.

questionText:
a. There are two similar tea bags. One is placed in a cup of hot water while the other is placed in a cup of cold water.
i. In which cup will the water turn brown more quickly? (1 Mark)
ii. Explain your answer to part i with reference to the movement of particles. (2 Marks)
b. A solution of copper (II) sulphate in water is saturated at 70°C. What will happen if the solution is cooled to 20°C? Give a suitable reason for your answer. (2 Marks)
sloText: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of diffusion in liquids and on the solubility and crystallisation of salts.
checkingHints: Part a.i (1 mark): In the cup of hot water.

Part a.ii (2 marks): 1 mark for stating that higher temperature increases the average kinetic energy and speed of water and tea particles; 1 mark for stating that faster particle movement increases the rate of diffusion.

Part b (2 marks): 1 mark for stating that excess copper(II) sulphate solute will crystallise / precipitate out at the bottom; 1 mark for explaining that solubility of CuSO4 decreases when temperature is lowered from 70°C to 20°C.

rubric.description: Part a.i: Identifies the cup of hot water.
Part a.ii: Explains that heat increases molecular kinetic energy and velocity, resulting in faster diffusion of tea particles.
Part b: States that crystals of copper(II) sulphate will form / settle out.
Part b: Explains that solubility of CuSO4 in water decreases upon cooling from 70°C to 20°C.

modelAnswer:
a.i. The water will turn brown more quickly in the cup of hot water.
a.ii. Explanation: At higher temperature, water molecules and soluble tea particles possess higher average kinetic energy and move much faster. These rapid random collisions cause the dissolved tea particles to spread (diffuse) from the tea bag throughout the bulk water at a much higher rate.

b. Effect of Cooling Saturated Copper(II) Sulphate Solution from 70°C to 20°C:
- Observation: Blue crystals of excess copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4·5H2O) will separate out and settle at the bottom of the container (crystallisation).
- Reason: The solubility of copper(II) sulphate in water is directly proportional to temperature. When the saturated solution is cooled from 70°C to 20°C, the solvent's capacity to hold dissolved solute decreases significantly, forcing the excess dissolved solute beyond the 20°C saturation limit to crystallise out.

questionText:
During an experiment, MgBr2 and NaCl salts in their molten form are electrolysed in separate electrolytic cells.
Illustrate the reaction at anode and cathode in each electrolytic cell using balanced chemical equations.
a. MgBr2 (2 Marks)
   At the anode:
   At the cathode:
b. NaCl (2 Marks)
   At the anode:
   At the cathode:
sloText: Write balanced ionic half-equations for electrode reactions during the electrolysis of molten salts.
checkingHints: Part a (MgBr2) - 2 marks:
- Anode (oxidation, 1 mark): 2Br^-(l) -> Br2(g) + 2e^-
- Cathode (reduction, 1 mark): Mg^(2+)(l) + 2e^- -> Mg(l)
Part b (NaCl) - 2 marks:
- Anode (oxidation, 1 mark): 2Cl^-(l) -> Cl2(g) + 2e^-
- Cathode (reduction, 1 mark): 2Na^+(l) + 2e^- -> 2Na(l)  (or Na^+ + e^- -> Na)

rubric.description: Part a Anode: Writes balanced oxidation half-equation 2Br^- -> Br2 + 2e^-.
Part a Cathode: Writes balanced reduction half-equation Mg^(2+) + 2e^- -> Mg.
Part b Anode: Writes balanced oxidation half-equation 2Cl^- -> Cl2 + 2e^-.

modelAnswer:
a. Electrolysis of Molten Magnesium Bromide (MgBr2):
- At the anode (Oxidation of bromide ions):
  2Br^-(l) -> Br2(g) + 2e^-
- At the cathode (Reduction of magnesium ions):
  Mg^(2+)(l) + 2e^- -> Mg(l)

b. Electrolysis of Molten Sodium Chloride (NaCl):
- At the anode (Oxidation of chloride ions):
  2Cl^-(l) -> Cl2(g) + 2e^-
- At the cathode (Reduction of sodium ions):
  2Na^+(l) + 2e^- -> 2Na(l)   (or Na^+(l) + e^- -> Na(l))

questionText:
Give reasons why:
a. Mercury is used in thermometers. (1 Mark)
b. Silver is used in making jewellery. (1 Mark)
c. Copper is used to make water pipes. (1 Mark)
d. Reaction mixture of sodium and water turns red litmus paper to blue. (1 Mark)
sloText: Relate the physical and chemical properties of metals to their practical uses and chemical reactions.
checkingHints: Part a (1 mark): Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature, is a good conductor of heat, and has a uniform/high coefficient of thermal expansion (and does not wet glass).
Part b (1 mark): Silver is a lustrous shiny noble metal that is malleable, ductile, and resistant to corrosion/oxidation.
Part c (1 mark): Copper is malleable/ductile, strong, and unreactive with water (resistant to corrosion/rusting).
Part d (1 mark): Sodium reacts vigorously with water to form sodium hydroxide (2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2), which is a strong alkali/base that turns red litmus paper blue.

rubric.description: Part a: Mentions uniform thermal expansion, good heat conductivity, and liquid state across a wide temperature range.
Part b: Mentions attractive metallic lustre, malleability/ductility, and low reactivity (corrosion resistance).
Part c: Mentions corrosion resistance in water, strength, and malleability to form pipes.
Part d: Explains formation of alkaline sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution.

modelAnswer:
a. Mercury is used in thermometers because it exists as a liquid metal over a wide temperature range, is a good conductor of heat, exhibits a uniform and high coefficient of thermal expansion with small temperature changes, is opaque/easy to read, and does not stick to (wet) the capillary glass wall.
b. Silver is used in making jewellery because it is a noble metal with an attractive white metallic lustre, is highly malleable and ductile (easily shaped into intricate designs), and is resistant to atmospheric oxidation and corrosion.
c. Copper is used to make water pipes because it is strong, malleable, and ductile (can be drawn into pipes easily), and lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series so it does not react with hot or cold water and resists corrosion.
d. Sodium reacts vigorously with water to produce aqueous sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas:
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
Because sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is a strong alkali (base) that releases OH^- ions in solution, the resulting alkaline mixture turns red litmus paper blue.

questionText:
In 1911, a scientist proposed planetary model for an atom based on the given illustration of gold foil experiment.
i. Name the scientist who carried out the gold foil experiment. (1 Mark)
ii. Based on the given experiment, describe the FIVE main points of the planetary model of the atom as concluded by the scientist identified in part i. (5 Marks)
iii. Mention the TWO fundamental defects in the planetary model of the atom. (2 Marks)
sloText: Describe Rutherford's gold foil experiment, the postulates of his planetary atomic model, and its fundamental defects.
checkingHints: Part i (1 mark): Lord Ernest Rutherford.
Part ii (5 marks - 1 mark for each of any 5 valid conclusions):
1. Since most alpha particles passed undeflected through the gold foil, most of the volume of an atom is empty space.
2. Deflection of a few alpha particles proves that all positive charge is concentrated in a central region called the nucleus.
3. Complete rebound of a very few alpha particles shows that the nucleus is extremely hard, dense, and carries almost the entire mass of the atom.
4. The size of the nucleus is extremely small compared to the total volume of the atom.
5. Negatively charged electrons revolve around the nucleus at high speed in circular orbits (like planets around the sun).
6. An atom as a whole is electrically neutral because the number of revolving electrons equals the number of protons in the nucleus.
Part iii (2 marks - 1 mark for each defect):
1. According to classical electromagnetic theory, a revolving charged electron should emit energy continuously and spiral/collapse into the nucleus, making the atom unstable.
2. If electrons emit energy continuously, they should produce a continuous spectrum, whereas atoms experimentally produce a discrete line spectrum.

rubric.description: Part i: Names Ernest Rutherford.
Part ii: States 5 main postulates/conclusions of Rutherford's planetary model (1 mark each).
Part iii: States the 2 fundamental defects—atomic instability (electron spiral into nucleus) and failure to explain line spectrum (1 mark each).

modelAnswer:
i. Scientist Name:
Lord Ernest Rutherford (1911).

ii. Five Main Points of Rutherford's Planetary Model of the Atom:
1. Mostly Empty Space: Since the vast majority of alpha (α) particles passed straight through the thin gold foil without deflection, most of the volume occupied by an atom is empty space.
2. Central Positively Charged Nucleus: The large-angle deflection of a few positively charged α-particles proved that all the positive charge of an atom is concentrated in a tiny central core called the nucleus.
3. Dense and Hard Nucleus Concentrating Mass: The complete rebound (180° bounce back) of a very small fraction (about 1 in 20,000) of α-particles showed that the nucleus is extremely dense, rigid, and contains virtually the entire mass of the atom.
4. Revolving Electrons (Planetary Orbits): Negatively charged electrons revolve rapidly around the central nucleus in circular paths (orbits), similar to planets revolving around the sun, such that centrifugal force balances electrostatic attraction.
5. Tiny Nuclear Size & Electrical Neutrality: The volume of the nucleus is negligibly small compared to the overall size of the atom, and the atom as a whole is electrically neutral because the number of extranuclear electrons equals the number of protons inside the nucleus.

iii. Two Fundamental Defects in Rutherford's Planetary Model:
1. Instability of the Atom: According to Maxwell's classical electromagnetic theory of radiation, an accelerated charged particle (revolving electron) must radiate energy continuously. Consequently, the revolving electron would lose kinetic energy, follow a shrinking spiral path, and ultimately collapse into the nucleus—yet real atoms are stable.
2. Continuous vs. Line Spectrum: If revolving electrons emit radiation continuously across all frequencies as they spiral inward, atoms should produce a continuous spectrum; however, excited atoms experimentally emit radiation only at specific frequencies, producing a discrete line spectrum.

questionText:
i. Name and describe the types of bonds and their formation in the following species. (7 Marks)
   I. A water molecule (H2O)
   II. A hydronium ion (H3O^+)
ii. Mention ONE similarity between the bonds identified in part i. (1 Mark)
sloText: Describe covalent and coordinate covalent (dative) bonding in water (H2O) and hydronium ion (H3O+) using dot and cross structures.
checkingHints: Part i.I - Water molecule (H2O) (3.5 marks):
- Identifies bond type as (polar) single covalent bond (1 mark).

- Explains formation: Oxygen (Z=8; valence 6 electrons) shares 1 electron each with two Hydrogen atoms (Z=1; 1 valence electron) to complete its octet and hydrogen's duplet, leaving 2 lone pairs on oxygen (1.5 marks).
- Draws accurate dot-and-cross or structural diagram of H2O (1 mark).
Part i.II - Hydronium ion (H3O^+) (3.5 marks):
- Identifies bond type as coordinate covalent (dative covalent) bond alongside covalent bonds (1 mark).

- Explains formation: Oxygen atom in H2O (donor) donates one of its non-bonding lone pairs of electrons to an electron-deficient hydrogen ion / proton H^+ (acceptor) which has an empty 1s shell (1.5 marks).
- Draws accurate dot-and-cross structure with arrow (->) from O lone pair to H^+ and overall +1 charge (1 mark).
Part ii - Similarity (1 mark):
- Both bonds involve the sharing of a pair of electrons between bonded atoms (and once formed, coordinate covalent and normal covalent O-H bonds in H3O^+ are identical in bond length and strength).

rubric.description: Part i.I: Names polar single covalent bond in H2O, explains mutual electron sharing between O and 2 H atoms, and draws dot-and-cross structure.
Part i.II: Names coordinate covalent (dative) bond in H3O^+, identifies H2O oxygen as lone-pair donor and H^+ as acceptor, and draws dot-and-cross diagram with dative arrow.
Part ii: States similarity—both bonds consist of a shared pair of electrons holding atoms together.

modelAnswer:
i. Types of Bonds and Their Formation:

I. Water Molecule (H2O) — Polar Single Covalent Bonding:
- Type of Bond: Single covalent bond (specifically polar covalent bond).
- Formation: An oxygen atom (8_O: 1s2 2s2 2p4) has 6 valence electrons and needs 2 more electrons to complete its octet. Each hydrogen atom (1_H: 1s1) has 1 valence electron and needs 1 more to complete its duplet. The oxygen atom mutually shares one electron with each of the two hydrogen atoms, forming two O–H single covalent bonds. Oxygen retains two unshared pairs of electrons (2 lone pairs).
- Structure: H : Ö : H (with two lone pairs on O), or H–O–H.

II. Hydronium Ion (H3O^+) — Coordinate Covalent (Dative) Bonding:
- Type of Bond: Coordinate covalent (dative covalent) bond (in addition to the two existing polar covalent O–H bonds).
- Formation: A hydrogen ion (proton, H^+) has lost its only electron and possesses a completely empty 1s valence shell. When H^+ approaches a water molecule (H2O), the oxygen atom acts as an electron-pair donor (Lewis base) and donates one of its two lone pairs of electrons to the vacant orbital of the H^+ ion (electron-pair acceptor / Lewis acid). This forms a coordinate covalent bond represented by an arrow pointing from oxygen to the hydrogen ion.
- Reaction & Structure: H2O + H^+ -> [ H–O(->H)–H ]^+ (with one remaining lone pair on O and a +1 charge on the ion).

ii. Similarity Between Covalent and Coordinate Covalent Bonds:
- Both types of bonds involve a shared pair of electrons localized between two atomic nuclei. Once formed, a coordinate covalent O–H bond is physically and chemically indistinguishable from a regular single covalent O–H bond in terms of bond length and bond energy.

questionText:
i. Describe the density of solids and gases based on the strength of intermolecular forces present among their particles. (4 Marks)
ii. Differentiate between amorphous and crystalline solids on the basis of the following properties. (3 Marks)
• Geometrical shape
• Melting points
• Symmetry
sloText: Explain the physical properties of solids and gases using intermolecular forces and differentiate between crystalline and amorphous solids.
checkingHints: Part i (4 marks):

- Solids (2 marks): Possess very strong intermolecular forces that pull particles tightly together with negligible empty space; therefore, a large mass is packed into a small unit volume, giving solids very high density.

- Gases (2 marks): Possess extremely weak / negligible intermolecular forces, allowing particles to move far apart with huge empty spaces; therefore, very little mass occupies a large volume, giving gases very low density.
Part ii (3 marks - 1 mark per property comparison):
- Geometrical shape: Crystalline solids have a definite, regular three-dimensional geometrical shape; Amorphous solids have no definite geometrical shape (irregular/shapeless).
- Melting points: Crystalline solids have sharp, fixed melting points; Amorphous solids do not have sharp melting points (they soften and melt gradually over a wide temperature range).
- Symmetry: Crystalline solids possess symmetry (regular repeating arrangement of particles in 3D); Amorphous solids are unsymmetrical (lack long-range order/symmetry).

rubric.description: Part i (Solids): Links strong intermolecular forces and tight particle packing to high density.
Part i (Gases): Links negligible intermolecular forces and large intermolecular spaces to very low density.
Part ii (Geometrical shape): Contrasts definite regular 3D geometry in crystalline solids with irregular/indefinite shape in amorphous solids.
Part ii (Melting points): Contrasts sharp fixed melting point in crystalline solids with gradual melting over a temperature range in amorphous solids.
Part ii (Symmetry): Contrasts presence of crystal symmetry in crystalline solids with absence of symmetry in amorphous solids.

modelAnswer:
i. Density of Solids and Gases Based on Intermolecular Forces:
- Density of Solids: In solids, the intermolecular forces of attraction between particles are extremely strong. These strong attractive forces pull the constituent atoms, ions, or molecules very close together into a tightly packed arrangement with almost zero intermolecular empty space. Because a large number of particles (high mass) are concentrated within a very small volume (Density = Mass / Volume), solids exhibit high density.
- Density of Gases: In gases, the intermolecular forces of attraction between molecules are negligible (extremely weak). Consequently, gas molecules move freely at high speeds and spread far apart from one another, creating vast empty spaces between particles. Because a very small mass of particles occupies a large volume, gases have extremely low density (about 1000 times less dense than solids and liquids).

ii. Differentiation Between Amorphous and Crystalline Solids:
1. Geometrical Shape:
   - Amorphous Solids: Do not have a definite geometrical shape; particles are arranged randomly in a disordered manner (shapeless/irregular, e.g., glass, rubber, plastic).
   - Crystalline Solids: Possess a definite, characteristic three-dimensional geometrical shape due to the orderly, repeating arrangement of particles in a crystal lattice (e.g., NaCl, diamond, quartz).
2. Melting Points:
   - Amorphous Solids: Do not have a sharp or fixed melting point; they soften and melt gradually over a wide range of temperatures.
   - Crystalline Solids: Have sharp, fixed, and well-defined melting points at which the entire crystal lattice breaks down abruptly.
3. Symmetry:
   - Amorphous Solids: Are unsymmetrical (isotropic) and do not possess planes, axes, or centers of crystal symmetry.
   - Crystalline Solids: Are highly symmetrical; when rotated about an axis or reflected across a plane, they show identical geometric appearances (planes, axes, and center of symmetry).

questionText:
Given below is zinc-carbon battery.
i. What is the anode, cathode and electrolyte made up of in the given dry cell battery? (3 Marks)
ii. How does the zinc-carbon battery work? Support your answer using balanced chemical equation for the reactions occurring at the anode and the cathode. (4 Marks)
sloText: Describe the construction, components, and electrochemical working (electrode reactions) of a dry cell (zinc-carbon battery).
checkingHints: Part i (3 marks - 1 mark each):
- Anode: Zinc metal cylinder / container (Zn).
- Cathode: Central carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by manganese(IV) oxide (MnO2).
- Electrolyte: Moist paste of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) and zinc chloride (ZnCl2) (mixed with MnO2 and starch).
Part ii (4 marks):

- Working description (2 marks): When the external circuit is connected, zinc atoms at the anode oxidise by losing electrons, which travel through the external wire to the graphite cathode where ammonium ions and MnO2 undergo reduction, converting chemical energy into electrical energy.
- Anode equation (1 mark): Zn(s) -> Zn^(2+)(aq) + 2e^-
- Cathode equation (1 mark): 2NH4^+(aq) + 2MnO2(s) + 2e^- -> Mn2O3(s) + 2NH3(g) + H2O(l)

rubric.description: Part i: Identifies Anode as Zinc (Zn) outer container.
Part i: Identifies Cathode as Carbon (graphite) rod.
Part i: Identifies Electrolyte as moist paste of NH4Cl, ZnCl2, and MnO2.
Part ii: Explains oxidation at zinc anode, electron flow through external circuit, and reduction at graphite cathode.
Part ii: Writes balanced anode half-reaction: Zn -> Zn^(2+) + 2e^-.
Part ii: Writes balanced cathode half-reaction: 2NH4^+ + 2MnO2 + 2e^- -> Mn2O3 + 2NH3 + H2O.

modelAnswer:
i. Components of the Zinc-Carbon Dry Cell Battery:
- Anode (Negative Electrode): Made up of the outer cylindrical Zinc (Zn) metal container.
- Cathode (Positive Electrode): Made up of a central inert Carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by powdered manganese(IV) oxide (MnO2).
- Electrolyte: A moist paste composed of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl), zinc chloride (ZnCl2), and manganese dioxide (MnO2) thickened with starch/water.

ii. Working of the Zinc-Carbon Battery and Electrode Equations:
- Working Principle: The zinc-carbon dry cell is a primary galvanic (voltaic) cell that converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction. When the positive and negative terminals of the battery are connected via an external circuit:
  1. At the anode, metallic zinc atoms have a higher oxidation potential and lose two electrons each (oxidation), forming Zn^(2+) ions that dissolve into the paste.
  2. The released electrons flow from the zinc anode through the external wire (powering the connected load/bulb) to the central graphite cathode.
  3. At the cathode, ammonium ions (NH4^+) from the electrolyte paste and manganese(IV) oxide (MnO2) accept these incoming electrons and undergo reduction to form manganese(III) oxide (Mn2O3), ammonia gas (NH3), and water (H2O).

- Balanced Chemical Equations:
  • Reaction at the Anode (Oxidation):
    Zn(s) -> Zn^(2+)(aq) + 2e^-
  • Reaction at the Cathode (Reduction):
    2NH4^+(aq) + 2MnO2(s) + 2e^- -> Mn2O3(s) + 2NH3(g) + H2O(l)
